title: Neurotechnology, Biotechnology and AI for Science
overview: From neural-signal acquisition to molecular design, experimentation and scientific discovery.

guide.objective: Understand two distinct convergences: neural signals decoded into device control, and AI models used to explore biological candidates that still require experimental validation.
procedure: Generate synthetic EEG data and inspect the two simulated classes.
Change acquisition noise, sample size and decision threshold; compare test metrics and ROC-AUC.
Inspect a test epoch and distinguish its true label, prediction and predicted probability.
Run an active-learning campaign and compare UCB with random selection under the same experiment budget.
Explain why an observed best candidate is not necessarily the candidate with the highest true activity.
guide.model: BCI: two synthetic EEG channels sampled at 128 Hz, 256 samples per epoch; logarithmic μ- and β-band power features; stratified 72/28 train/test split; standardization on training data only; regularized logistic regression. ROC-AUC groups tied scores correctly. Molecular candidates: normalized descriptors, an RBF-kernel Gaussian process and UCB acquisition μ(x)+βσ(x)−λR(x).
guide.limitations: No patient recordings or real molecules are used. Synthetic signal power is not clinical EEG. The NEO example is a specific clinical application; the simulator does not reproduce NEO or attribute accuracy metrics to it. The candidate model does not predict protein folding, binding affinity, pharmacology or clinical efficacy. Eight campaigns compare strategies; the best measured activity is not the hidden true activity.
questions: How does the decision threshold affect sensitivity and specificity?
Why can the best observed candidate be a noisy measurement?
What is the difference between exploration and exploitation in UCB?
What evidence is needed between computational prediction and clinical or industrial use?
guide.answers: Changing the threshold changes sensitivity and specificity, but does not change the score ranking and therefore does not by itself change ROC-AUC. A single high measurement may reflect noise. Active learning can improve sample efficiency, but does not guarantee that UCB beats random selection in every campaign.

slides.title: The New Frontier of Intelligence
slides.subtitle: Neurotechnology, biotechnology and AI for science.
slides.takeaway: How does a computational prediction become experimental evidence?
slides.notes: Opening slide. Introduce two converging but distinct frontiers: neural interfaces and AI-assisted biological design. Keep the distinction between prediction, experiment, regulation and scale visible throughout.

slides.title: Two Frontiers, One Evidence Cycle
slides.subtitle: Neural signals and molecules require different models.
items: Record signals, extract features and decode defined tasks.
Explore sequences, structures and molecular interfaces.
Risks, time scales, data and regulation remain domain-specific.
slides.takeaway: Methodological convergence does not erase biological differences.
slides.notes: In a BCI, activity is recorded and decoded to enable interaction. In biotechnology, AI explores molecular candidates and processes that must be validated experimentally. The sequence is conceptual, not a universal recipe.

slides.title: A Brain–Computer Interface
slides.subtitle: A neural signal becomes an action through calibration.
items: Non-invasive EEG, ECoG or intracortical recordings, depending on the device.
A model trained for defined tasks and users.
Cursor, prosthesis or glove; the user receives feedback.
slides.takeaway: A BCI does not mean unrestricted thought reading.
slides.notes: EEG is an indirect signal and is sensitive to artifacts. Implants require surgery and clinical evaluation. The laboratory uses synthetic signals, not patient EEG. The performance of a BCI depends on population, protocol, calibration and context.

slides.title: NEO: Bounded Clinical Evidence
slides.subtitle: A hand-motor function compensation system.
items: Epidural implantable interface with eight electrodes.
Decode motor intention and control a pneumatic glove.
Fudan reported registration approval in China in March 2026.
Defined use and indications; no universal recovery claim.
slides.takeaway: Separate device authorization, individual efficacy and access to treatment.
slides.notes: Nature Biotechnology reported on 17 April 2026 that China approved the NEO implant by Neuracle for a specific application in people with paralysis. The device records signals associated with intended hand movement; they are decoded to control a robotic glove. The report describes eight electrodes and an implant above the dura. Do not claim general efficacy or open-ended thought reading.

slides.title: China’s BCI Industrial Strategy
slides.subtitle: 2025 guidelines set targets for 2027 and 2030.
items: Seven government bodies published guidelines for the sector.
Technology, standards and two to three industrial clusters.
An industrial ecosystem and two to three internationally influential firms.
slides.takeaway: Official targets express policy intent, not achieved results.
slides.notes: The 2025 Chinese guidelines set goals for 2027 and 2030. Present these as official targets, not verified outcomes. The strategy combines sensors, chips, software, clinical evaluation, production and standards.

slides.title: From Biological Sequence to Product
slides.subtitle: AI accelerates exploration; experiments determine what works.
slides.takeaway: A predicted affinity is not an approved medicine.
slides.notes: The conceptual workflow is to identify a desired function, use sequence or structural information, generate candidates, synthesize them, and test activity, stability, safety and scalability. Do not mistake computational affinity for demonstrated biological performance.

slides.title: AiCE and Void-X
slides.subtitle: Two methodological contributions from CAS research groups.
items: Protein engineering that incorporates structural and evolutionary constraints into inverse-folding models.
A generative model for protein–protein interface design at atomic scale.
Identify the task, test set and experimental validation.
Demonstrate reproducibility and usefulness beyond the development set.
slides.takeaway: Two studies do not establish a general clinical platform.
slides.notes: AiCE was presented by the Chinese Academy of Sciences in 2025 as a protein-engineering strategy combining structural and evolutionary constraints. Void-X, from the Shanghai Institute of Organic Chemistry, was presented in 2026 as a generative model for protein–protein interface design. Distinguish methodological contributions from demonstrated commercial or clinical use.

slides.title: AI for Science
slides.subtitle: ScienceOne 100 and the augmented research cycle.
items: Prediction and design with explicit assumptions and uncertainty.
slides.takeaway: CAS announced ScienceOne 100 in April 2026; independent evaluation remains necessary.
slides.notes: AI for Science applies computational models, AI and automation to stages of scientific work; it does not remove critical judgment or experimental validation. CAS announced ScienceOne 100 in April 2026 as a system of specialized models and tools for multidisciplinary research.

slides.title: Adoption, Risks and Limits
slides.subtitle: Maturity stages are not interchangeable.
items: Proof of concept and method validity.
slides.takeaway: Neural privacy, biosafety and reproducibility cut across the entire cycle.
slides.notes: Use an evidence-and-maturity matrix. Research is not a product; regulatory authorization is limited to the approved use; industrial scale requires stable production, cost control, access and productivity. Discuss neuroprivacy, informed consent, dual use, bias and traceability.

slides.title: Five Takeaways
slides.subtitle: Neurotechnology and biotechnology are converging frontiers, not automatic promises.
items: Signal and data quality condition every inference.
AI expands the search space but also introduces error and uncertainty.
A useful prediction requires physical or biological validation.
Economic advantage requires production, regulation and adoption.
Privacy, safety, access and reproducibility matter.
slides.takeaway: Which links in these value chains could Argentina and Latin America develop?
slides.notes: Close by distinguishing research, validation, industrialization and outcomes. Invite discussion of regional capabilities: bioinformatics, clinical trials, biomedical data, agricultural biotechnology, protein design, instrumentation and digital services.
